Siralim 2, developed by Thylacine Studios, is what happens when you mix the grind-heavy heart of classic RPGs with the creature-collecting fun of Pokémon—then crank the complexity to 11. Released in 2016, it doesn’t just lean into old-school aesthetics; it weaponizes them, delivering a hardcore, addictive, and surprisingly rich experience.

This is a game for players who want more. More monsters. More loot. More mechanics. More of everything—and it delivers.

At its core, Siralim 2 is a turn-based RPG where you summon and control a team of up to six creatures to battle through procedurally generated realms. Your character—the ruler of the titular kingdom—can harness the power of over 600 different creatures, each with unique abilities and synergies.

Combat is strategic and fast-paced, but don’t let the simple visuals fool you—there’s a staggering amount of mechanical depth. Each monster can be customized with artifacts, spell gems, breeding combinations, and even mutations that fundamentally alter how they perform in battle.

You’ll explore endless dungeons, complete quests, fight bosses, and hoard mountains of loot. There's no level cap. No final floor. It just... keeps going. And weirdly, that’s the appeal.

The real magic lies in Siralim 2's endless progression systems:
-Creature Breeding: Combine two creatures to create powerful offspring that inherit abilities and stats from both parents. Breeding isn’t just for stronger creatures—it’s for building entire team strategies.
-Artifacts and Spell Gems: Equip monsters with customizable gear and magic. Every item can be upgraded, enchanted, or transformed. The combinations are nearly limitless.
-Castle Building: Upgrade your kingdom to unlock new features, vendors, and mechanics. The castle evolves with your choices, turning it into a hub of power.

Graphically, Siralim 2 is unapologetically retro—think 16-bit era pixel art. It’s functional, not flashy, but the visual simplicity allows the gameplay systems to shine. Animations are basic but snappy, and UI design, while dense, becomes intuitive once you settle into the rhythm.

The soundtrack is atmospheric and loops comfortably in the background, doing its job without stealing the show. Like the visuals, it’s more about utility than flair.

What separates Siralim 2 from other monster battlers or dungeon crawlers is its freedom. You can min-max until your brain melts or casually explore new realms and experiment. There's no wrong way to play—just infinite ways to tweak your build until it becomes absurdly broken.

That said, it’s not for everyone. There’s minimal story. The learning curve is steep. And the grind? Absolutely real. But if you thrive on number-crunching and system mastery, this game is a dream come true.

Pros:
-Massive roster of customizable monsters
-Deep and complex combat system
-Endless progression with no true “endgame”
-Great replayability and team-building experimentation
-Ideal for fans of min-maxing and theorycrafting

Cons:
-Graphics may be too dated for some
-Minimal story and character development
-UI can feel overwhelming early on
-Grind-heavy progression loop

Siralim 2 is a monster-battling sandbox that rewards curiosity, experimentation, and obsessive tinkering. It's not about saving the world—it's about bending it to your will through strategic brilliance and absurdly optimized teams. If you're the kind of player who enjoys finding broken combos and watching your enemies melt, Siralim 2 might just become your next obsession.

Hardcore, nostalgic, and ridiculously deep—Siralim 2 is a genre-defying gem for players who love systems over spectacle.

If you enjoy JRPG style grinding, dungeon crawling, monster collection, and party management, then you'll love the Siralim series. Siralim 2 looks similar to the first aesthetically, but it adds a lot of new features and some quality-of-life changes. The new features feel like natural evolutions of the first game, so I like them. This is the kind of game you can sink dozens, or even hundreds, of hours into. 

Do note, the mechanics are a lot different from other RPGs/roguelikes you may have played. In the very early game, you might find yourself stuck in a battle because the enemy creature's trait is stacking their defense to infinity. That brings me to an important point, you need to be able to be okay with dying, possibly a lot. Some bosses have abilities that seem unwinnable if you don't scout them and find what strategy you need to win. If you tend to blunt force one strategy and save scum all the time, you might not like this game.

There's lots of cool monsters, and the deities you meet all have interesting personalities. As long as you don't take it too seriously, the writing in this game is pretty funny and engaging. I recommend asking each deity to describe their realm, some of them have compelling stories even though they're all short.

This game isn't for everyone, but old school dungeon crawler fans should enjoy it.

Howdy folks, you may remember my name from a time where I first stepped my foot into the budding series of Siralim with it's first game, of course named, Siralim. Due to the nature of how this series evolves I am gonna preface that there is really not much to say, but that's a good thing, as most of the things that there are to say are, quite frankly, very good.

As far as sequels go, Siralim surprised me as every game I noticed the positive ratings and overall reception only went up and up, and it really shows as the quality of the game only manages to match that pattern. From the 1st game to the 2nd game the amount of refinement was honestly impressive for such a small indie game. Many systems that were convoluted or overbearing were cut out and other systems that just needed some work got the love and care they needed to be fun and worth the engagement. Not to mention brand new systems like the amazing monster breeding. Albeit it has an annoying mechanic tied to it that really slows it down and makes it a tedious task should you want to do it a lot, Power Balance. However I won't rant too much on it as Power Balance as a whole is completely removed in Siralim 3, thankfully.

That being said however, it's honestly a deserved level of praise I give the series as Siralim is probably one of the few series I can remember where I played a game for days, finished it, and then started the next game almost instantly to then repeat the pattern. A lot of times when I discover a series and it has several games I'll beat one, take some time away, and then come back to it later on. I did this for the first Siralim as I really enjoyed it but it had a lack of polish in many areas. Siralim 2 however really raised the torch and it's no wonder that the polish only goes higher in the next game, and now the franchise has a 4th entry called Siralim Ultimate that just released not 10 days prior to this review that I've heard many amazing things about.

Siralim is one of those series where the games don't deviate too much from the core concept and quite frankly you could very well skip over the earlier ones and jump straight to the brand new toys and tricks, but being the completionist I am, I always like to take a trip back and see where the roots of something started before hitting the grand conclusion. In a way it gives a level of understanding and nostalgia as you slowly see how something went from ambitious ideas to completely owning the concept it set out to create. It's a very magical feeling to sit back and remember all the good times along the way. 

All and all I have nothing short of praises to sing for Siralim as a series, should you seek to undertake my suggestion of digital stimulation, I do declare you could go on much worse rides than the onslaught of creatures and mayhem this suspiciously good series has to offer. 

Stay safe and enjoy farming Power Balance if you start your new (or returning) journey into the world of Siralim.

Went into this one expecting a Pokémon like dungeon crawler but gave up after spending a good day with it. My major complaints with the game were that it's repetitive, lacks overall polish and that the battles rely too much on random outcomes. You can probably read about the upsides in other reviews, so I'll focus here on what turned me away from the game.

[b]many mechanics, too many perhaps?[/b]
The game has very many, perhaps too many, different mechanics, terms and concepts that you need to learn, most of which can be scaled or modified numerically in some way by yet other mechanics. Basically anything that you encounter in the game at first has multiple better versions of it. Some pruning and refining would go a long way. It's start off nice and gently with a tutorial but then quickly resorts to just leaving you to read a bunch of manuals. These would be nice if they were supplementary, but the UI lacks basic functionality like hovering over an icon for a status effect like "poisoned" or "shielded" to get an explanation of what it does. Instead you have to resort to memorizing effects and consulting said manuals [i]after you encountered them in a fight[/i].

[b] too many random effects [/b]
While all the different monsters and mechanics make for a combinatorial explosion of team compositions, I found myself wondering how much of it is really meaningful – many of the effects are random and thus harder to build a strategy around. In addition the effects themselves often seemed negligible: what does a 10% chance to hit for 10 additional damage do if my monster's base attack is already 50? The pervasive reliance on randomness in battle effects is a deterrence for me more so than an upside. The only time I was ever challenged in my playtime was when I came up against a gang of monsters that frequently turned invisible, and thus ravaged my party because I couldn't retaliate against them. On closer inspection it turned out that the monsters had a mere [i]chance[/i] to turn invisible after each attack and I just got unlucky for multiple turns in a row.

[b] repetitive, but not so engaging [/b]
Traversing the actual (randomly generated) dungeons feels lackluster and samey. The floor layouts do not differ drastically from floor to floor and the different tile sets (forest, beach, crypt) do very little to disguise this. Basically it's the same endless dungeon that just goes deeper and deeper with no overworld or connecting parts. There's are many different flavored events (read: different text boxes) that all just put some stuff in your inventory. The dungeon floors are strewn with collectibles and treasure chests, but picking it all up is just busy work for the sake of busy work. And there's never a reason to not pick anything up. In fact anytime you collect even a minor resource, it brings up a menu instead of simply adding it automatically to your collection by walking over it – just one small example of how the interface could be improved.

In my entire playtime I didn't even lose a single battle, in fact the encounters seem to become (relatively) easier as my monsters grew in level. The enemy AI didn't seem particularly clever, but it's hard to judge with all the random effects and my team always having the numbers advantage. I could of course dive one dungeon level deeper and the hopes of encountering a challenge there, but ultimately, I just don't see a reason to come back and keep exploring.

[b]obnoxious Steam achievements[/b]
This is one of the games where the developers uses achievements to meticulously track your progress through the game, so be prepared for a lot of annoying pop ups. Unfortunately I couldn't just turn off the Steam overlay because I was playing with the Steam controller :(

Siralim 2 is a turn-based, party-based game which boasts immense diversity in pretty much everything it does. There is also a strong breeding component furthering the collection mechanic. There is a short campaign, but for the most part it seems designed to facilitate near-endless play. Diversity may be found in creatures (same creatures in your 6-man army as well as your foes), artifacts (each creature may hold one), spell gems (each creature may hold one), main character development and on, and on.

Pros:
[list]
[*] Great flexibility in everything. You can build things just they way you want (eventually). The way the core systems interact is very nice.
[*] Mechanism by which you level-up your character is interesting (you need to do favors for gods, which amounts to basically interacting with objects/winning fights.)
[*] Team building is fun, though initially you are greatly restricted by the creatures you have access to.
[*] There is lots do to outside of combat (crafting, breeding, leveling up artifacts, tinker with spell gems, leveling up your main character).
[/list]

YMMV:
[list]
[*] There is no structure in what you are supposed to do. By the time the very short main campaign has been completed, you have barely scratched the surface of things you can collect/upgrade/accomplish. After a while, you feel you are like playing just to play, with no real goal in mind. This may be fine for some, but this lack of purpose is what ultimately led me to quit.
[/list]

Cons:
[list]
[*] Core fighting experience starts out nicely, but ultimately becomes trivial. Soon you are fighting just to grind. You want the fights to be over as fast as possible (a design element the game seems to encourage), to level up, to collect more, to increase your favor with gods and so forth. Lost in this is the fact that the grinding grows old at some point. Most fights are over before they begin by equipping gems which activate at the start of the fight.
[*] No support for mouse. 
[*] You are limited in your ability to breed by "Power Level". I actually kind of like this system, but it is too restrictive in its implementation.
[*] Any need for deeper strategy and tactics may be overcome by simply breeding what seem to be exponentially stronger characters, as a function of their "gene strength".
[*] The main action takes place in "realms". There are plenty of diverse objects to interact with in the 15 different realms (each led by the a different god). However, for the most part, this interaction is nothing more than bumping into the object and possibly then bumping into another object.
[/list]

I'm giving this game a hearty thumbs up. I think I'm done with it. I'm sure I have no where come close to completing it. I will probably never return to it. So why the hearty thumbs up?

Well every previous old school simplified platformer game I have tried before has lost me literally in 15 minutes or so. Just too boring. Sure there is some nostalgia to the idea of playing a relic of a game but that fades super fast once you try. As a kid I played so much pac man on the old ataris that I could get nearly infinite lives. Last year I went to an adult throw back arcade and after 10 minutes on pac man I was wondering how in the world I ever played it so much as a kid. Same goes for these old school games.

This game hooked me though. after 15 minutes, when I should have been uninstalling it, it was just deep enough to make me want to go a little longer. After a couple hours I was all in on creating the perfect little monster army! That is the key to this game. The levels are all the same with slightly different skins. You fight the same simplified battles over and over. There is only a few simplified quests at a time. On the surface, there simply isn't enough here to justify playing this game.

Thankfully there is a lot below the surface. There is a huge variety of monster types with a wide variety of individual or party effects. Then you can breed them to create upgraded versions and "new" varieties. 
Next you can equip them with an artifact which comes from a nice selection of types of artifacts. However artifacts level up and you can upgrade, update, enhance, and otherwise buff your artifacts.
Next you can customize your monsters further by equipping them with spell gams of your choice rather than having to be locked into specific spells per monster. 
Next you have access to three different perk trees to further enhance your monsters or character specific buffs.

Add all that to a bunch more below the radar content and you have a pretty deep squad development game. It isn't about clearing the levels, or the combat, or the quests. It is all about being able to build and develop your own unique monster squad tailored exactly to how you want to build it. And thus, you have a real gem here for people who like that sort of thing. That's also why there is no need for me to finish, or be investd in the story or any such nonsense. I completely enjoyed the part of the game that was meant to be fulfilling and it was well worth the money for how it played out.
I guess I played this game a little bit. It's pretty good, you should buy it.

A game wonderfully designed for those with a tinkering mindset. If you enjoyed building up a pokemon team or a cohesive fire emblem force, Siralim 2 offers a unique experience; you travel pocket dimensions, where your team of up to 6 creatures fights another group of up to 6 creatures in turn-based combat. 
In combat, your creatures can attack, cast spells you selected for them, increase their defense, provoke the enemy (making them more likely to be targeted by the enemy) or extract a core from the enemy (effectively capturing them, and allowing you to summon one of the monsters later from the hub world). 
From this relatively simple basis, the game offers a staggering amount of customization: each creature species has a unique passive ability (called a trait) that gives them some special edge. Traits can change the way a specific debuff works, gives the creature a buff or changes how it casts spells, defends etc. In addition to the creature specific trait, you can give each creature an artifact to hold that changes their stats, allows them to inflict specific debuffs when they are attacked or when they attack AND can also grant them another trait. Each artifact a creature carries gains experience as it is used in combat and each time it increases in level it becomes more powerful and can hold more upgrades. Each creature can also hold a number of spell gems, drawn from a shared pool based on a creature class (Life, Nature, Death, Sorcery or Chaos), spells each have their own effects BUT they also have inherent modifiers to make each one unique. Some spell gems have a change to automatically cast themselves on a critical hit, on a specific action or at the start of battle, others can be cast on multiple targets, cost less mana or even cost no mana and instead cost HP.
New creatures can sometimes be found and extracted from in battle, but you can also breed two of your summoned creatures together creating a new offspring creature. Doing so increases the ‘Gene Strength’ of the resulting creature, making it stronger than normal. As you go deeper and deeper into the pocket dimensions the enemies become stronger and stronger.

There is even more than this, each realm has a specific patron deity who you can please by accomplishing missions, there are rewards and special monsters to gain by doing so. You expand your hub castle and gain new services, options and modifiers.
The game shines brightest when you are seeking out creatures that synergize well together to create a party that is nigh unkillable, then facing a tense battle where the party you face seems just as well designed.
Suffice it to say. If this sounds interesting to you, I advise you to RUN not walk to the store page and check it out.
My only real gripes about the game are that it requires a LOT of wiki searches if you want to do things in an optimal fashion and if you build a team with a lot of automatically casting spells (like I did) then expect for there to be a LOOOOOONG wait at the start of a battle if you cast 8-9 spells in a row.

If you don’t mind a bit of grinding, and lots of experimentation, this game is a great way to spend a lot of time! All in all I give it a: 9.2/10.
Also, check out the sequel! I certainly am.

If you're looking for a great, time-consuming game, and are a fan of vintage RPG's, this game is for you. If you love collection-type games, such as Pokemon or Monster Rancher, this game is for you. I bought it on deep sale, totally on a whim, and have found it to be a captivating game. 

It reveals layers slowly, and at your pace, based on how you unlock new features and perks for your character, which often come with gameplay quirks of their own. While the story isn't particularly deep or nuanced, you will most certainly get your value, even if the game was bought at full price.

It particularly appeals to the crowd that loves to micromanage their party; you'll always find something to optimize. You will always have a goal to work toward. The content is seemingly endless. There's literally hundreds of monsters and thousands of breeding combinations. There's countless options toward optimizing your party, your equipment, your castle, and your character.

This game is perfect for playing while listening to podcasts, as the sound is basic, and nothing is lost by muting it entirely.

There's a reason why this game has even been ported to consoles; it's that good, despite its basic visual look. The gameplay is solid, and honestly is better than even some AAA titles I've played in my life.  You owe it to yourself to try this game if anything I have to say about this title appeals to you.

I have a bit of a love/hate relationship with this game. I just changed it from a positive to a negative.

On the plus side, there is no end to the amount of stuff you can do in this game. Creatures, artifacts, spell customization, rep grinding... it literally never ends. The graphics might be old-school, and some of the monsters look downright goofy, but the newer ones look pretty awesome. This game was developed by one guy as far as I know, and I really respect the level of care he put into it.

On the down side, I keep encountering crashes, corrupted saves, and some combinations of spells can cause your gameplay to freeze up. The technical stuff brings this game down, and it's a shame, because when it works its tons of fun.

I would recommend it, but be sure to back up your saves, both on the cloud and on your hard drive. I've had to delete all my files multiple times just to get the game to run, and I would have lost everything had I not copied the saves onto my desktop first. Buyers beware.

Siralim 2 was my choice for the first game I'd purchase on Steam. My background: I'm a huge sucker for anything with fantasy creatures and my favorite franchise is Pokemon. I also play a lot of the old (GBC) Dragon Warrior Monsters games and a bit of Digimon (the Stories games with the turn-based combat).

So, I'm biased. This is important, as this is gonna be a very positive review, BUT I want to preface it by saying this: Creature collecting and breeding games in the line of Dragon Warrior Monsters hinge on grinding. Your goal is to create the strongest monsters/parties possible and you'll go through the same motions over and over trying to achieve that goal. No matter how positive my review, assess for yourself wether that's your thing or not. 

Onto the review:

Story: Siralim 2 features a very basic, quest-based story. The game tells you upfront that the story is not the main focus, just a little pointer, so you can familiarize yourself better with the gameplay loop and your castle. Usually, you'll be given the location of the next story-based encounter in one or two text boxes and that's basically it, you're on your own again, trying to get to the level ("realm") the story encounter resides in. Nothing much to see here, really. The story is serviceable at best and forgettable at worst. It does provide *some* entertaining dialogue though.

Gameplay Loop: The gameplay loop is as follows – you gather up 6 creatures, venture into a procedurally generated dungeon (top-down view) and venture through the realms, which is what the game calls its floors. On each floor, you'll encounter a deity that'll provide you with realm quests – little fetch quests to keep you busy. These yield hefty rewards – ressources for castle/facility building and usage, artifacts to equip your creatures with, spell gems, even new creatures at certain points. You also find tons of destroyable objects that either yield favor points for the realm deity or ressources. For me personally, this is great – it keeps me engaged as I look for the next shiny trinket. The rewards are same-y and plentiful, but that's what makes it feel good. Also, all that stuff goes towards building your party, so that's awesome! 

Battle: Battles are a turn-based affair with a simple, almost spartan looking menu. I think the font used for the entire gameis Arial and it doesn't look very aspiring at all. It does it's job though – turn order and party status are visible at all times and you can easily check buffs/debuffs and creature traits by the press of a button. When things get going, it *can* get a little hectic in terms of text speed. I use a party of 6 where 2 monsters use auto-activation spells while DoT statuses proc constantly and it honestly becomes a bit disorienting at times. It becomes better the more you familiarize yourself with how your party works, but it's something to keep in mind. By the way, I mentioned traits: These are basically personal abilities of each creature – like in Pokemon! Traits are handled like real game changers. So far, barely any ability was "just there"– everything matters. My Wolpertinger slings free spells whenever it attacks or gets attacked, while my Brownie Brute just happens to deal AoE damage with each normal attack. On the other hand, the wights can just come back to life after being slain and swampdwellers come with extremely bloated stats that decrease over time. It makes for very exciting battles that can easily end in your demise if a trait just happens to counter your overall team plan – like party-wide silencers for example. 
Fortunately, defeat isn't as brutal as it sounds – you don't lose unsaved progress. You do get sent back to the castle and your power (a percentage meter used for various activities like traversing the dungeon or summoning creatures) gets set to the starting value of 100%.
Overall, I really enjoy the battle system. It's classic, it's snappy and it just feels satisfying. Also, your creatures have little sound effects when attacking. I love my Brownie Brute's crazy cackle – it gives them personality. By the way – I know people have said the battle system was slow. Personally, I don't think it is at all. There's an option to speed it up even more, but from what I saw, it's perfectly reasonable. If you played DWM 1, it feels similar to that.

The castle: Now to the "boring" part – micro management! Whenever you aren't killing off creatures in the realms, you'll be here. Vendors, the shrine, the breeder and the stables are here among other things. You can even play little minigames that usually revolve around a meter and hitting a certain point on it. Think golf games. These are honestly not very engaging, but luckily, there isn't a need to do them either. Other than that, outfitting your creatures is VERY needed. You'll unlock facilities as you progress and later will be able to upgrade them at your leisure by venturing out. All of them are easy to understand and well explained. There's even a library with all the info in your menu or physically in the castle. It has a list of all the debuffs, buffs, traits, whatever you might need info on. The descriptions are curt but VERY to the point. Exact percentages are a min-maxer's dream and you got it all in here. The game basically brings its own GameFAQs with it – the FAQs anyway, not the boards.
The customization options you unlock range from naming your creatures, upgrading and creating artifacts to even changing your character's appearance. Nothing of that has relevance to gameplay, but I feel reminded of games like Disgaea for such neat details. Meet Baseball, the Crypt Bat, and shiver in fear!
In all seriousness though, the game wants you to micro manage and provides EVERYTHING needed. You can even register equipment sets, so you can re-assign your healer's artifacts and spells with one click after re-breeding them. The game oozes of QoL features like that.

The creatures: This game boasts 600 of them. And while they in general look very nice and varied, you *do* notice that a lot of partial palette swaps are involved. The Sand Giant is a beige giant. The wall giant is that same creature, with a brick wall pattern. The mutated Vampire Bat is just a Vampire bat with foam around the mouth. Stuff like that is a detractor, especially early on when only a few creature types are available. I did notice though, that even though this trend never completely stops, the sheer variety of creature types and tribes, as well as the details on later creatures in a tribe help alleviate the problem. Still, keep this in mind.
I also noticed that some of the creatures just look very blobby and flat, while others are extremely detailed and well-made. The difference between a Bile Slime and a Doom Fortress is a bit jarring, which is sad as slimes usually count towards my favorites. For future installments, I'd really suggest the developers to adhere to a consistent style. Just "retro pixel art" is not enough of a definition, there's certain levels of quality and this game's creature sprites are not on a consistent level.

Sound and SFX: I mentioned creature sounds before and still find them very charming. The sound design in general is very classic, but fitting. If you played some RPG maker games, you kinda know what to expect, as it's nothing out of the ordinary. What IS nice though, is that both SFX and BGM can be regulated independently. I usually listen to my own music while grinding, so this was very welcome.

Overall: I'm rather new on Steam – I only created this account... a month before writing this review, not even. I bought Siralim 2 almost immediately and I haven't seen the need to buy anything else yet. This game has me addicted with its fun and rewarding gameplay loop and has me caught up in real nostalgia. If you are looking for that and monster management, go ahead, this is the perfect game for you on Steam. Just keep in mind that the monster designs aren't as refined as one would wish.

Fantastic game. Don't let appearances deceive you here. This is a very deep and complex experience. I don't write many reviews, but this gem deserves it for sure. I'll give you a quick rundown on what this game is, what it does well, and then some things I think could be improved upon (very nitpicky, and very few) Here goes!

Siralim 2 is a monster catching, pixel art, turn based RPG. Having never played Pokemon I couldn't tell you how similar they are but I have seen the two compared online. So you catch monsters (by extracting their cores) and then you can summon them at your castle and use them in your team. Each monster has a unique ability that will define the way you use it. And these aren't tiny number buff here and there, they are game changing. For instance a Fallen Carnage's unique trait is that every time it kills an enemy creature, it fully heals, and can then immediately take another turn. Monsters are separated into "families" if you will. And seem to be centered around a theme. Using the Carnage family as an example, they all center around things happening after your guys kill an enemy. Oh and there are ~600 monsters total in the game. 

So you have your monster team, and have a stable of a few back up creatures. Now what? You can breed them. All of them. And the offspring can be many times stronger than the parents if you do it right. As you continue to experiment, you'll build your library of "recipes" and will soon be able to pick and choose what creatures you want to start building the ideal teams to take out specific boss battles and high tier dungeons.

Every creature can equip an item, that is customisable with many different attributes and skill depending on how you want to build your team. They can also equip spell gems that let them use a wide variety of skills in battle. And these systems are just as deep as the breeding if not more so.

The rest of the game is engaging as well. You can upgrade your castle to gain access to different crafting stations (a chef to cook meals for you and your team that give you temporary buffs while exploring, a smith to forge new artifacts for creatures to equip) and improve existing ones. There is a pantheon of gods and goddesses in the game that you earn favor with and get 'Deity Points' when your reputation ranks up, that you can then spend on passive skills for your mage class (there are 5) as well as your creatures, and generic character skills as well. There is a ton to do and upgrade. And it all changes the gameplay loop in some way.

To conclude, this is one of the best value for money games I have come across especially in recent years. No level caps, the game scales for as long as you want to play it. You can even upload your PC save to the cloud and then download it onto the mobile version (iOS and Android) to keep playing while you're at wor... I mean "on the go". The depth is there and you are given so many ways to play its mind boggling. The few complaints I have: 1) The UI can be a bit of a chore. It's old fashioned and a bit ugly, but it gets the job done. 2) The Power Balance mechanic is more of a hindrance than anything else (thankfully the dev has promised this mechanic is gone in Siralim 3 which is currently in development) but as it stands it's not breaking the experience for me personally though your milage may vary. And that's it! If you want to see the game in action with a commentary geared to beginners check out this youtube series by Warlord Mal. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aUBFWDbEHEE Thanks for reading!

Siralim 2 is pretty much the ultimate creature game. There are some "baseline" combos (hunters, hounds, etc.) that are obvious... but there are also some combos that are much, much, much, much better.  For one example, there's a creature that, on death, deals damage to enemies based on its max health... and another creature that combines the max health of ALL 6 of your creatures, and assigns that total to each creature but makes them take extra damage.  Such combos can be extraordinarily fun to come up with and execute.  This, combined with your personal character upgrades, artifacts, spell gems, etc. results in an incredibly deep and complex layering of ways to make you feel strong.  There's just a lot of content in this game, and it is more than worth the full 15 bucks they're asking.  Plus, apparently there's a mobile version of it that you can sync up and play on the pooper, which is always nice. With that out of the way, Siralim 2 is a Turn-Based RPG based around gods and creatures. One of said gods is you, the player. In terms of difficulty, most of the challenges you'll encounter in your adventure come from a need to level up to beat bosses or perhaps find a new team composition to clear realms quicker. As I stated before, anything can become OP when used correctly, so it is extremely fun to experiment with different creature combinations and team compositions.

Siralim 2 is a combination monster catcher, castle management, and semi-roguelike RPG. You begin by selecting from one of five types of mages: Life, Nature, Chaos, Sorcery, and Death. After a short introduction, you find yourself at your castle with lots of stuff to do. 

You can teleport to a realm, which is a contained random map with enemies, treasures, and one of 15 gods with whom to gain favor. Gaining favor with the various gods gives various perks and access to new cores.

Cores can be extracted from most creatures, though there are some (such as those gained by earning favor with the gods) can only be purchased. From the beginning, you can only extract cores from the base creatures. Once you have bred or summoned a creature, you will be able to extract cores from creatures like it that you find in the wild. The creature count (with the expansion) is somewhere around 700 different creatures you can have (with no limits on how many of each).

Breeding is done one of two ways. You can pick the parents yourself, or you can use recipes you have found while exploring realms. Breeding creatures gives them an increase in power, so even breeding two of the same creature together can be beneficial as they become more and more powerful. The only drawback to breeding is that you are limited by your Power Level, which is increased through combat and has a maximum of 200%, minimum of 20% (there are also fairies you can use to give you a boost to Power Level). Since breeding costs 50%, you can only breed three creatures before needing to increase your Power Level again. Still, it is lots of fun to breed new creatures and see them show up in the game world (where you can now capture their cores).

There are many more things to do, and with 40 hours in the game, I have only scratched the surface. You can craft artifacts to equip on your creatures and give them special boosts. There are many spell gems that can be equipped and modified with special bonuses (such as automatically being cast when your creature is hit). You can cook different foods to give special bonuses. Recruit villagers into your castle who give you various quests, along with a tailor who can craft costumes for you. Plus more.

Combat is not just about dealing a lot of damage. Each creature has a trait which can greatly change the course of battle, so you will need to prepare for anything. I had to forfeit battle against a much weaker creature because my party could only deal physical damage, and this particular creature casts Shell on itself each time it takes damage. Shell prevents all damage from the next attack against it. If I had equipped a single damage spell, I would have been able to defeat it, but even my much stronger creatures were useless against it. 

The bosses are also difficult and unique. I have only fought through to the 19th-level boss, which is difficult because it requires your party to be able to survive for a long time (unless you just happen to guess the correct combination). My "all-powerful" team of level 30+ struggled against this boss.

Siralim 2 is a pretty interesting RPG.

Difficile de comprendre exactement ce qui accroche autant sur ce jeu. On ne peut pas dire qu'il est beau, il est répétitif et l'histoire n'as aucun intérêt, la conception des niveaux est très moyenne y compris au niveau de la génération aléatoire et le jeu n'as simplement pas grand chose pour attirer l'oeil.

Mais derrière tout ces points négatifs, il s'agit simplement du meilleur jeu de capture et de combats de créatures auquel j'ai joué. Le côté répétitif permet d'essayer une infinité de variations dans ses stratégies et n'impose aucune limite à notre entraînement. Le jeu est extrêmement riche, le nombres de possibilités est impressionants et on a toujours l'impression de découvrir de nouvelles choses, de trouver de nouveaux objectifs et de nouveaux défis.

En bref, le mauvais côté du jeu, c'est qu'il ne consiste qu'à répéter les mêmes choses à l'infini, mais ce qui fait sa richesse, c'est l'incroyable nombres de variations qu'il est possible de s'ouvrir dans cette répétition. Si on accroche, ne serait-ce qu'un peu au système de jeu, alors on ce lassera difficilement de jouer avec tout les jouets que nous donne le jeu...
